newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudanese conflict puts dusty town in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Sudanese conflict puts dusty town in spotlight.

text.p: The town gates marking the entrance to the city where Sudan government forces are massing to counter a rebel offensive say "Come in peace".
But the truckloads of young Sudanese volunteer fighters who arrived in Damazin on Friday and Saturday have other ideas.
"America is a liar. Hurray Sudan," shouted the men, carrying blood-red flags symbolising war, from their perch on top of a truck loaded with dates and goats.

Officials at the checkpoint entrance to this southern city about 530 km (330 miles) south of Khartoum said the men were first-time volunteers in the Sudanese People's Defence Forces which have joined the army in its latest fighting with rebels.
Some soldiers wore plastic sandals with their fatigues and others acted shyly, retreating behind comrades when a vehicle of foreign journalists approached.

The officials said the group was heading to the southern front in Sudan's war against the rebels, including the Sudan People's Liberation Army which has been fighting the Islamist dominated government since 1983.
Sudan accuses Eritrea in the east and Ethiopia in the south of abetting the rebels, a charge both countries deny. It has also said that it expects a third front to open on its border with Uganda.
Khartoum maintains that the United States supports all three countries.

This dusty town, where cattle graze along unpaved streets and cone-shaped grass huts outnumber the simple mudbrick, came into the picture because of its proximity to the Roseires Dam, which provides 80 percent of Khartoum's power.

The rebels say that they are advancing on Damazin, rather than Khartoum, to put pressure on Sudan's Islamist government and spark a popular uprising -- the method by which the Sudanese people have brought down other governments.
At the strategic Roseires Dam near the Ethiopian border, Sudanese officials scoffed at what they said were the latest claims by rebel leader John Garang that his troops are 20 km (13 miles) away.

On top of the dam, journalists saw only the effect of what the massive, rust-red wall can do -- tame an enormous lake of water on one side into a gentle creek which meanders along a bed of polished rocks and lush banks.
But the hydroelectricity plant, which an official in Khartoum said has seven 30-megawatt turbines, and the dam appear to be reinforced.
At sundown, soldiers on top of the dam sat on blankets on the ground next to anti-aircraft guns and shared a meal ending their daily fast in the Moslem month of Ramadan.
